summary:
We built Pleiades to help future astronauts plan journeys across Mars with a clearer understanding of the effort, time and oxygen they may need. Our aim is to make resource limits part of route planning from the start.

Users select a starting point and destination on an interactive map. The system combines estimated walking effort and oxygen use into a cost map, then calculates a route based on those priorities. Users can explore the result in 2D or 3D and review estimated distance, travel time and oxygen consumption. Adjustable oxygen budgets and reserve settings help them assess whether a journey fits their available supplies.

Our main contribution is bringing route visualization and resource planning together in one interface. The current prototype uses simulated inputs and simplified assumptions, so its estimates still need validation against real measurements. It provides a working foundation for testing how different planning choices affect a proposed mission.

Next, we plan to connect physical sensors, improve radiation-risk estimates with NASA solar-activity data, and add AI-assisted anomaly detection and recommendations. We will also evaluate whether atmospheric drag has a meaningful effect on route calculations. Our long-term goal is to help crews make informed decisions during Mars surface missions while keeping the resources needed to return to base in view.
details:
Pleiades is an interactive prototype for planning astronaut walking routes on Mars. We built it to help users understand how a journey may affect their time, physical effort and oxygen supply, and to make resource limits part of route planning from the beginning.

Users select a starting point and destination on a map. The system combines estimated walking effort and oxygen consumption into a weighted cost map, which guides route calculation. A color-coded heatmap and interactive 2D and 3D views help users explore the result. The 3D view represents the model’s calculated cost, rather than measured terrain elevation. The interface also displays estimated distance, travel time and oxygen requirements, with adjustable oxygen budgets and reserve settings.

The main benefit is bringing route selection and resource planning into one clear interface. Users can see how a proposed journey relates to their available supplies before committing to it. Our intended impact is to support informed decisions during future Mars surface missions, with the resources needed to return to base considered throughout the planning process.

We used NASA Mars Trek to explore Martian imagery and maps as references for the prototype. Supporting tools included Canva for the presentation and OpenAI Codex for assistance with writing, translation, presentation revisions and the project’s video-sharing webpage. That webpage uses HTML and CSS. Physical sensor integration is a future development goal; the current prototype uses simulated inputs and simplified assumptions.

The creative aspect of Pleiades is its focus on the person making the journey. By connecting movement effort, oxygen use and visual route planning, we turn abstract resource estimates into information that users can explore on a map. Our team considered walking difficulty, journey duration, oxygen availability, reserve requirements, map scale and uncertainty in the underlying estimates.

The current version demonstrates this approach, but its predictions still need testing against measured data. Our next steps include connecting real sensors, improving radiation-risk estimates using NASA solar-activity data, and adding AI-assisted anomaly detection and recommendations. We also plan to evaluate whether atmospheric drag meaningfully affects route calculations. These improvements will help us refine the model and assess its usefulness for future mission planning.
